content:
Marketing has tolerated bluffing for too long.

 

Now even excellent marketers are paying the price.

 

I don't have first-hand experience (yet) of what Mark Ritson describes, but I believe it.

 

In another study, Ritson found that 65% of marketers lack even the most basic marketing knowledge.

 

Would we accept the same elsewhere?

 

A software engineer who doesn't understand software fundamentals.
A finance professional who doesn't understand basic finance.
A product manager who doesn't understand UX.

 

Probably not.

 

Of course, every profession has weak practitioners.
But marketing has been unusually tolerant of fluffy language and sloppy or outsourced execution.

 

That was always a weakness.
And now the chickens are coming home to roost.

 

Marketing is becoming far more complex, technical and competitive.

 

Consider digital marketing.
Traditional marketers may still know little about it, yet digital now occupies perhaps 90% of CEOs' agendas.

 

Meanwhile, marketing is climbing the executive agenda.
"marketing is too important to be left to the marketing department", the quote goes.
So CEOs have less patience for impressive vocabulary without real expertise, especially in digital.

 

A study by Boathouse found that only 32% of CEOs trust their CMOs.
No wonder. And it is highly problematic.

 

Marketers who have never got their hands dirty or understood digital, let alone AI, certainly won't improve that trust.
No surprise some are struggling to find work.

 

But others already occupy senior seats and, aware of the changing market, are unlikely to leave.
That reduces turnover and senior openings, blocking even excellent marketers caught in broad layoffs, restructuring or similar circumstances.

 

Marketing is not changing.
Quite the opposite: its fundamentals couldn't be more relevant today.

 

It's the skills of the people doing marketing that are, or should be, changing.
